articles.title: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102
articles.summary: Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later life. Eva Marie Saint – a life in pictures. Her best films – ranked.
body: Eva Marie Saint, one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and 50s, has died aged 102. Her screen work spanned six decades: Saint made her screen debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, starred in Alfred Hitchcock’s celebrated thriller North by Northwest, and in one of her last screen appearances played Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero film Superman Returns.
A family spokesman said on Tuesday that Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles.

Born in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer that was chronicled in a 1949 feature in Life magazine which started with the prophetic words: “The name of Eva Marie Saint may someday be a household word” – it followed her struggles to gain a foothold in the entertainment industry. By the early 50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play The Trip to Bountiful.

articles.title: George Cheeks Addresses Staffers in First Memo as Skydance TV Co-Chair: ‘CBS Remains a Cornerstone’
articles.summary: George Cheeks, newly appointed to the role of Skydance TV co-chair and chief content officer, laid out his vision to staffers Tuesday, as the $111 billion merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed.
body: “The work ahead is significant, and so is the opportunity,” he said in the note. “I am energized by the possibilities. Together, we’ll build on our collective strengths to create an even stronger future.”

Cheeks’ ascension at Skydance was a huge vote of confidence from Ellison, who had previously tapped the exec to serve as Paramount TV media chair last year when Skydance first took control of Paramount. Prior to that, Cheeks was one of the three co-CEOs of Paramount Global (previously known as ViacomCBS) — and was the only one of that triumvirate to make the transition to the new company.

Today is the start of a new chapter. By bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, we’ve assembled a remarkable collection of television brands, networks and studios, backed by some of the most talented teams in the industry.

I want to acknowledge the hard work, creativity and dedication you each bring to this historic moment. Thank you for playing through the noise this past year. I am excited to move forward together and shape our future as one team.

articles.title: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire
articles.summary: New York film festival: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield. On the day that Luca Guadagnino ’s film about Sam Altman and OpenAI premiered, Vanity Fair released a cover story on Altman.
body: How much worse can things get? AI agents have already gone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases. Last year, a young woman used ChatGPT as a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life.

Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studios pulled out of distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick. Neither does it have much to say about the world – glossy magazines included – that has welcomed them with open arms.

articles.title: Unions and Democrats Stump for Federal Film Incentive: ‘We Are So Close to Getting This Done’
articles.summary: A delegation of California Democrats campaigned with union leaders on Tuesday for a federal film incentive as they seek to build momentum to pass the measure by the end of the year. Sen. Adam Schiff and eight Democratic representatives from Southern California argued that the U.S.
body: They will have about five weeks during the lame-duck session of Congress after the election to try to pass the bill. Rep. Laura Friedman, whose office organized Tuesday’s press conference, said she is “cautiously, guardedly optimistic.”

“We need to have this on the president’s desk by mid-December, as far as I’m concerned,” she said in an interview, adding that she hopes the bill will pass in essentially its current form as part of a larger tax package. “This has been almost two years of constant work. It hasn’t just come together in the last few weeks. It’s been a snowball effect. It started out as this idea, and then we just kept building and building and building. So I feel like we have a great momentum.”

The proposal includes a 5% bonus for filming in a disaster area, which would apply to the entirety of Los Angeles County until January 2030, due to last year’s fires. There are also bonuses for independent films and for filming in rural opportunity zones. The total tax credit could rise to 50% or more when combined with state incentives in places like California and New York — easily surpassing the incentives offered by other countries.

articles.summary: An artisanal café in a quiet yet fashionable Seoul neighborhood provides the setting for a quartet of seasonal vignettes in Kim Jong-kwan’s romantic anthology “The Table: Day and Night.” Opening this year’s Busan Film Festival, the film — with its star-studded ensemble including Kim Min-ha, Shim…
body: In this year's Busan festival opener, director Kim Jong-kwan assembles a starry cast for a quartet of romantic interludes set in the same Seoul coffee shop, but the concept overpowers the stories themselves.

The first chapter, titled “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” details the fairytale meeting between two customers, Hyeon-oh (Joo Jong-hyuk), a young man with a passion for rebuilding old watches, and Yoo-jin (Kim Min-ha), a forlorn dreamer, whose inherited antique timepiece has not worked in years. “Still Ourselves,” the second vignette, treads a precarious line between comic and tragic, when Young-min (Chang Ryul) is accosted by the beautiful yet increasingly unstable Sang-mi (Han Sun-hwa), a former middle-school friend who accuses him of not remembering her, before begging that he protect her from an encroaching unseen enemy.

articles.title: ‘I’m bringing together women who nourish me’: French film-maker Alice Diop on her debut installation
articles.summary: The Saint Omer director has gathered work by artists, writers, composers and poets for Geste de Consolation, set in the 60m-long central hall of the Palais d’Iena in Paris. Alice Diop has just returned to France from California when we speak.
body: Diop had been attending a two-week celebration of her work organised by the French department at University of California, Berkeley, in which academics pored over her documentaries ( Nous (We), Vers La Tendresse (Towards Tenderness)) and her first feature film, Saint Omer, which received the Silver Lion in Venice in 2022. The courtroom drama was inspired by a real trial that Diop attended, of a Senegalese woman who had allowed her baby to drown in the sea. Over two hours, it explored the complexities of race, culture and motherhood in contemporary France. The film was the first by a black female director to be entered by France as its official entry in the 2023 Academy Awards.

“To be studied like that, in such a temple of intellectual resistance, I was bowled over,” says Diop of UC Berkeley. “As a film-maker, it’s not up to me to analyse my work. But listening to them, it was good to feel understood.”

articles.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
articles.summary: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
body: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.

The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.
It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.
The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.

articles.title: Axe used by Jack Nicholson in The Shining for sale as part of Stanley Kubrick auction
articles.summary: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive. A special effects axe wielded by Jack Nicholson as he delivered his chillingly manic line “Here’s Johnny!” in the 1980 horror movie The Shining is to go on sale.
body: Nicholson’s character, Jack Torrance, uses an axe to hack out an opening in a locked door protecting his terrified wife Wendy, played by Shelley Duvall. It is also the murder weapon in the killing of Scatman Crothers’ character, Dick Hallorann. One of cinema’s most famous axes could be yours for a list price of between £30,000 and £50,000.
It is one of hundreds of items in the first auction of the personal archive of The Shining’s influential director, Stanley Kubrick, who died in 1999.

The sale includes several other lots from the film, including two sky-blue dresses worn by the twin sisters Alexa and Alexie Grady. They appear in the frocks in a memorable scene when they invite Torrance’s son, Danny, to “come play with us” as he pedals on his tricycle through the corridors of the Overlook Hotel.

The boy’s trike is not part of the sale, but a clapperboard used in the film is one of four from Kubrick’s movies to go under the hammer. The others are are from 2001: A Space Odyssey, the 1975 historical drama Barry Lyndon and Kubrick’s last film, Eyes Wide Shut.
points: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive.

articles.title: The Lanterns Finale Explains Why There Are Multiple Green Lanterns From Earth
articles.summary: The final episode of Lanterns Season 1 finally answers a question fans have had since James Gunn's Superman: how can there be two Green Lanterns from Earth?
body: This article contains spoilers for "Lanterns" Season 1, Episode 8, "Dirt and Stars."

The first season of "Lanterns" has come to a close. This was an ambitious gamble on behalf of DC Studios, a show set in the same universe and continuity as "Superman," building up to John Stewart appearing in "Man of Tomorrow," that also introduced one of the biggest and most complex corners of the DC Universe. Rather than attempt to make a massive space-set show on a budget, "Lanterns" takes a "True Detective" approach and focuses on an investigation that deeply rocks its two leads, centering on character rather than action or even worldbuilding.

Not to say that "Lanterns" doesn't reference or touch on the larger Green Lantern world, of course. The show references Mogo and also Ch'p, while repeatedly teasing Sinestro's Yellow Lantern Corps and other-colored lanterns.
points: The final episode of Lanterns Season 1 finally answers a question fans have had since James Gunn's Superman: how can there be two Green Lanterns from Earth?
